Roland Hayes's public concert

With his accompanist Reginald Boardman, from New Hampshire, Hayes gives a concert that draws the largest crowd ever assembled at the college: three hundred outside guests, including 30 to 40 Black people, about 400 listeners in all. Lowinsky himself chooses the student ushers, instructs them to be extremely courteous and to answer the question of where to sit with “Wherever you please.” No incident despite the integrated seating; at the reception, one white woman remarks to another that times have changed.
near Asheville, North Carolina

One evening in mid-June 1945, Wunsch is arrested outside Asheville, parked in his roadster with a sailor; the charge: “crimes against nature,” carrying a mandatory prison sentence. Wunsch, driven by an instinct for self-punishment typical of homosexuals before Gay Liberation, immediately pleads guilty. Influential friends apparently intervene with the judge; the charge is reduced to trespassing and Wunsch is given a suspended sentence. John Andrew Rice would remark years later that the judge, a sensible man rather than a good judge, let the matter go.
Near Asheville, in his parked car

A faculty member, Wunsch is arrested for sexual intimacy with an American Marine in his car parked near Asheville — possibly a police setup to bring down the “nigger-lover” Wunsch. After a suspended sentence obtained by influential local friends, with no support from his colleagues, he has to leave the school in disgrace.
